France and Germany want the European Union to reach a deal in the next month on its 2028-2034 budget and financing for Ukraine ahead of a slew of elections across the bloc in 2027, but leaders made little progress on Thursday as discussions grew heated.
While the ​next EU budget only ‌starts in 2028, leaders want a deal by year-end because France, Italy , Poland , Greece , Estonia , Finland and Slovakia all hold elections next year, which ⁠could complicate negotiations on the almost €1.6 trillion ($1.8 trillion) draft budget that pays for all of the EU's key policies.
The seven-year budget requires unanimous approval from all 27 member states.
The possibility that French far-right leader Marine Le Pen , who leads in the polls, becomes president after elections in April ‌and May has focused minds. Le Pen has vowed to end financial aid to Ukraine, which is still fighting to hold back the Russian advance, and slash French contributions to ⁠the EU budget.
French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters that he had until the end of the year to strike a deal.
"After 31 December, I will no longer be in a position, politically or democratically, to reopen discussions on the budget and bring them to a conclusion, as we will be ​entering a period far too close to the presidential election in France," Macron said.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also mentioned the end of the 2026 as the deadline that leaders were ‌working towards.
The talks on Thursday, while inconclusive, are to help the chair of EU summits, Antonio Costa , present a budget proposal in the coming weeks on which EU governments might agree at a meeting on December 17 and 18.
"Even negotiations that do not lead to the desired outcome or the most positive result possible are necessary to make progress," Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker told reporters. "Even though we were apparently ‌unable to bridge our differences today, we may know what is necessary to ensure success next time."
Under the current proposal, the seven-year budget totals €1.582 trillion, which includes €140 billion to repay pandemic-era borrowing. The biggest line item is around €740 billion to support European farmers and help ​the poorest regions of the EU catch up with the richer ones.
Leaders must also sort out how to continue financing Ukraine as Kyiv defends itself against a Russian invasion that started in 2022.
The 2028-2034 budget draft includes up to €100 billion for Ukraine, which diplomats say falls well short of the country's needs.
The talks also cover aid to Kyiv in ​2027 because a proposed loan intended to raise funds for Ukraine would be borrowed against the EU's current budget, which expires at the end of next year. The EU wants to borrow €45 ​billion and lend it to Ukraine , to be repaid only when Russia pays war reparations.
In 2027, non-EU countries such as Britain, ​Norway, Japan , Switzerland and Canada are expected to provide another €25 billion for Ukraine. The combined €70 billion would cover the funding gap that Ukraine faces next year.
One of the fights is over whether all EU countries should contribute to the €45 billion ​loan to Ukraine.
Slovakia, the Czech Republic , Hungary and Bulgaria object, but Germany and several other countries have made participation a condition of a broader budget deal.
"For me, there is a link between our support for Ukraine and the European budget," Merz said. "The European Union comprises of 27 member states, not 23 or 24."
The four objecting countries are major net beneficiaries of EU spending. The debate is a microcosm of ongoing divisions between countries that contribute more to the EU budget than they get from it, such as Germany, Sweden , the Netherlands and Finland , and those that on balance receive more ⁠than they pay.
The net contributors want EU budget reductions, which would lower their contributions, and urge that spending prioritise making the EU more competitive against rivals like the US and China rather than subsidising European agriculture and poor regions.
The net ⁠beneficiaries say that the budget should ​have money for both aims, and believe doing that would sustain public support for the EU in the face of far-right political parties' rising popularity throughout Europe.

Iran denied responsibility on Thursday for drone strikes on Kuwait that killed two Italian nationals, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi calling the accusations baseless and proposing a joint investigation with Rome and Kuwait City.
Araghchi spoke by telephone with his Kuwaiti and Italian counterparts, Sheikh Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah and Antonio Tajani, and later wrote on X that the incident was "suspicious and looks like a preecooked recipe for war."

Senior spokesperson for Iran's armed forces Abolfazl Shekarchi flatly denied any Iranian military operation in the region and accused the US and Israel of staging a false flag attack to destabilise the area.
IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency went further, citing an unnamed security source who alleged that Ukraine had deployed a network of thousands of drones across the region, including in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. It provided no evidence.
The Iran embassy in Rome separately issued a statement categorically rejecting any Iranian role and warning against attempts to widen the war.
Saudi Arabia called for an immediate halt to Iranian attacks and said it held Tehran responsible for the consequences of its actions. Bahrain asked the UN Security Council to hold Iran accountable and demanded compensation for the damage.
Qatar warned that repeated strikes on Kuwait risked undermining diplomatic efforts to reduce regional tensions. The UAE, Syria and Jordan also condemned the attack.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called for increased pressure on Tehran and said Gulf security was directly linked to Europe's security.

Tehran has urged its neighbours not to allow their territory to be used for attacks against Iran.
Iran's army confirmed a separate drone attack on Kuwait's Ali Al Salem base earlier in November.
Tajani had informed the Italian parliament on 8 October of a decision to relocate most of its troops from Kuwait, with only around 10 military personnel remaining in the country at the time of the attack.

Iran has openly claimed its strikes on Gulf states throughout the war. So why is it denying an attack on Kuwait?
Two Italian technicians have been killed in a drone attack on a military site in Kuwait on Thursday, the first European civilians to die amid the United States-Israel war on Iran.
Kuwait and Italy have both blamed Iran. Tehran, which has for the most part not denied, outright, strikes on US military assets hosted by its Gulf neighbours and described those attacks as self-defence, has this time denied any role and has suggested the strike was a “false-flag” operation.
The denial has raised two questions: Who was behind the attack and, if it was Iran, why is it not taking responsibility?
On Thursday, several drones targeted military installations in Kuwait, according to Italy’s Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani.
Kuwait’s army initially described the target only as a “vital site”. Tajani later told the Italian Senate that it included an air-defence detection station where two technicians from Rheinmetall Italia, the Italian arm of the German defence company, were working.
The men were named by Italian media as Antonio Saccoccio, 65, from Formia, and Emanuele Lo Russo, 36, from Rome. They were maintaining detection antennae for the Skyguard air defence system used by Kuwait’s armed forces.
They were killed by falling shrapnel after the drones were intercepted, according to Kuwaiti and Italian reports. A Kuwaiti and a Pakistani national were injured.
The two dead men are the first European civilians to be killed as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran since it began in late February. A French soldier was killed in a drone attack in Iraq in March.
This was the first fatal strike on Kuwait in several months, although the country has been one of the hardest-hit Gulf states during the war. Its oil facilities, power infrastructure and airport have all been targeted at various points in the conflict. An Indian traveller was killed and 63 people were injured when drones hit Kuwait international airport on June 3 .
Both countries have blamed Iran for Thursday’s drone strike.
Kuwait’s Foreign Ministry condemned what it called a “sinful” attack and said the country reserved its right to take all measures to protect its sovereignty and the security of its citizens and residents.
After a call between Kuwait’s foreign minister and Tajani, the Kuwaiti ministry said the two had jointly condemned the strike.
Tajani told the Italian parliament the drones were “of Iranian origin”. The Gulf Cooperation Council’s secretary-general, Jasem Albudaiwi, also condemned what he called a “brutal attack”.
“The incident is suspicious and looks like a pre-cooked recipe for war,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X.
Araghchi called both his Kuwaiti and Italian counterparts to deny Iranian involvement and offered to mount a joint investigation, according to Iran’s foreign ministry. As of Thursday evening, Kuwait had not publicly commented on the call with Araghchi.
Armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi, speaking for both the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the regular army, said Iranian forces had conducted “no military or offensive operations whatsoever” in the region. He called the attack a “false flag” operation, while a military statement accused the US and Israel of using it as cover for continued aggression.
The Iranian embassy in Rome said it “categorically rejects the allegation”, suggesting the attack could have been staged to drag Europe into the Iran war.
The denial stands out because Iran has rarely disowned its attacks since US-Israeli strikes began in February. In November alone, it issued five statements claiming strikes on neighbouring states, four of them on Bahrain and Kuwait.
Tehran usually tries to justify those strikes as self-defence, arguing that it targets US bases from which Iran is attacked, not the countries that host them.
This is not the first time Iran has denied an attack on Kuwait, however. When a power and desalination plant was hit on March 30 , killing an Indian worker, Iran also claimed that Israel was responsible.
Hassan Ahmadian, a professor of Middle East studies at the University of Tehran, said Iran’s record of claiming its strikes should be taken seriously.
“Whenever the Iranians do something, they announce it,” he told Al Jazeera. “This time, as on three or four occasions during the war, they said, ‘This wasn’t us.'”
He argued that Iran would have little reason to hide this attack. “They’ve struck the Americans,” he said. “Would they be afraid to announce they’d hit Italians?”
Ahmadian said other parties in the region, such as Israel, might want to “complicate the situation” by blaming Iran, which he called “the ready-made party to blame”. He added that some in Iran also suspect Ukraine, which he argued has been trying to raise its strategic value to Washington.
As the US ran down its stock of expensive Patriot missile interceptor systems against a barrage of cheap, mass-produced Iranian Shahed drones, Ukraine offered its expertise to the US in March on how to combat the drones, which are also used by Russia.
Ahmadian said US involvement could not be ruled out either. Iran has previously told regional governments that the US was behind strikes on two sites during the war, he said.
“We’re looking at someone fishing in troubled waters. Otherwise, if it were the Iranians, they would have announced it,” he added.
Paolo von Schirach, president of the Global Policy Institute and a professor of political science at Bay Atlantic University in Washington, dismissed the idea of US involvement.
“It’s bizarre to suggest the United States would coordinate this attack on Kuwait, an ally in the Gulf, just to stir up feelings,” he said.
Von Schirach noted that Italy has refused to join the US war on Iran and does not support it. “Italy isn’t on America’s side in this conflict,” he said. “So we shouldn’t take this seriously.”
Muhanad Seloom, a senior non-resident fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, said it was important to “separate Iranian-made from Iranian-launched and Iranian-ordered”.
Tajani described the drone as Iranian-built, of a type also used by Iran-backed militias. Seloom said that makes an Iraqi armed faction the leading alternative suspect. Such groups have claimed attacks on US forces in Gulf states since the war began.
He called Yemen’s Houthis “a distant second” and said Tehran’s own suspects, the US, Israel and Ukraine, “come with no evidence”.
“Only debris, radar tracks and a launch point can settle it,” he told Al Jazeera.
Seloom said Tehran first used it in March over strikes on Turkiye, Cyprus and Azerbaijan . However, he said that The Soufan Center, a US-based security think tank, found that it failed to convince Baku.
Claims have run the other way, too. The best known was the reported arrest of Mossad agents plotting bombings in Qatar and Saudi Arabia, which came to nothing, Seloom said, because neither of those governments stood behind it.
“Alleged often, verified never, as far as I can establish,” he said. “What this war has is deniable action. Hiding the author is common. Framing someone else has yet to be shown.”
In the case of Thursday’s attack, he said, Iran’s false-flag claim “stands without evidence so far”.
Abdullah al-Shayji, a professor of political science at Kuwait University, said Iran’s narrative “doesn’t come close to being rational or acceptable”.
“Iran bombed us eight days ago, on the 18th of this month, and didn’t deny it,” he said. He said Iran had fired 925 missiles and drones at Kuwait since the start of the war, and more projectiles at Gulf states and Jordan than at Israel. “This doesn’t fool anyone,” he said.
Al-Shayji said the denial comes down to who was killed and where. “Italian technicians were killed, and not at a US base,” he said.

The presidents of France and Bulgaria have condemned violence that broke out at a Europa League fixture between Marseille and Levski Sofia in the Stade Vélodrome.
Television footage showed Marseille fans cornering a group of Levski supporters in the stands before beating them relentlessly, including with a belt. One Levski fan is seen bleeding from the head as he receives multiple blows while trying to protect a female friend. Reports from inside the stadium on Thursday suggested violence began after a Levski supporter was seen making a Nazi salute.
The Marseille prosecutor’s office said it would open an investigation into the trouble, specifically accusations that French fans committed “aggravated intentional violence” against Levski supporters, and that it would also pursue allegations of “incitement to hatred after Nazi salutes and provocations from the Bulgarian fans”.
A statement on behalf of the French president, Emmanuel Macron, on Friday said he condemned the violence “in the strongest possible terms” and that it had “no place in sport or in public places”. He also insisted “these acts would not go unpunished”.
The Bulgarian president, Iliana Iotova, described the violence as “unacceptable” and “shocking” and said: “The attacks against the Bulgarian fans desecrate one of the great games that brings millions of people together around the world. Everyone should be able to support their team without being afraid for their safety.”
The country’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, said he had spoken to Macron about the incident which had resulted in 11 Bulgarian fans being hurt, five of whom were taken to hospital.
“We share the position that aggression and violence have no place in civilised Europe,” Radev said. “I thank President Macron for his personal commitment to this case, for the medical care provided to the injured by the French authorities, for the measures taken to ensure the safety of Bulgarian citizens, and for the perpetrators to be held accountable.”
Another Europa League fixture on Thursday, between Besiktas and Hapoel Beer Sheva, was suspended for 30 minutes owing to fighting. Uefa’s account of the disruption that occurred at a neutral venue in Batumi, Georgia, said the game had been suspended to allow local police to subdue fighting between Besiktas supporters. Besiktas condemned what it called “disproportionate force” by security staff and said some fans had been denied entry.
Turkey’s football federation strongly condemned what it described as “unacceptable” actions undertaken by Georgian police targeting Besiktas supporters who unfurled a pro-Palestine banner during the match.
A Uefa statement, however, said: “Uefa understands that the escalation between the local police and Besiktas’ supporters – which caused the temporary suspension of the match – started following an intervention of the local police in the sector of the Besiktas supporters to neutralise clashes that had erupted amongst Besiktas’ own supporters.”
Uefa condemned the violence at both matches and said it had appointed inspectors to conduct disciplinary investigations. “Uefa competitions are founded on the principles of respect, fair play, integrity and safety,” a statement said. “The events witnessed at the above-mentioned matches run counter to these fundamental values.” Any investigation would “examine all available evidence to establish the relevant facts and circumstances”, the statement said.
Last season Marseille were hit with a partial stadium closure after fans launched fireworks and pointed lasers into the field during a Champions League fixture against Atalanta.

Jangling keys has turned into a symbol of protest against Spain's housing struggles
Spain's main party leaders have made their last pitch to voters in a fractious final TV debate that focused heavily on the country's housing crisis.
Spaniards go to the ballot box on Sunday, with opinion polls suggesting Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will fail to extend his eight years in office.
The debate on Thursday night marked the culmination of a campaign, which has been defined by the din of house keys being jangled in symbolic protest, rather than any carefully crafted words of politicians.
The struggle many face in opening the door to an affordable home has led to demonstrations filling plazas across the country.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo of the conservative People's Party (PP), who is poised to replace Sánchez, told viewers he would build a million new homes.
The PP, which is narrowly projected to be the largest party, is poised to form a government with the Vox party which is polling in third place.
If Vox do win a share of power at a national level, it would be the first time for the far right in Spain's 50 years of democracy since Francisco Franco's dictatorship.
Vox's leader Santiago Abascal told the debate only he cared about those who had the greatest housing need.
Ada Colau, who heads a left-wing coalition of four small left-wing parties called Broad Front, said taxing rich and exploitative landlords was urgently required.
Rejecting criticism that he had failed to tackle the country's housing problem, Sanchez talked up his recent emergency measures designed to protect tenants and cap rents.
Spanish elections: What you need to know and what's at stake
Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election
Sparking the protests in September was the eviction – and subsequent death in hospital – of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal (no relation to Santiago). She could not afford a tripling of her rent in Madrid.
But it is Spain's third city, Valencia, that is at the heart of what many call a full-blown housing crisis.
"We want to live together but we look at the prices of property and it's impossible," says 25-year-old Nuria Cifuentes from the city.
She and her boyfriend Miguel Martínez work as sports journalists but are still living with their respective families because of the high cost of renting a flat, even with their combined salaries.
Nuria and Miguel want to live together but feel they are priced out
"Half of what we earn would go on rent of more than €1,000 a month," Miguel, 26, says.
We meet the couple outside Valencia's futuristic science museum, whose distinctive design is often compared to the skeleton of a whale.
This coastal location has witnessed the biggest rise in rent prices of any major Spanish city over the past half a decade, according to official data from the INE, the national statistics office.
One study from the city's Polytechnic University put the increase at 78% between 2020 and 2025.
Sánchez called a snap election after Congress rejected his emergency housing reforms.
A revised version was later pushed through a parliamentary standing committee – restricting evictions and capping rent rises – but opponents say he has had eight years to sort the problem and has resolutely failed.
Nuria and Miguel say the soaring cost of housing means that life is on pause for them, as they're unable to make concrete plans for the future.
"Maybe we want to have kids, maybe we want to actually buy somewhere, but there are so many unknowns that all I see is a black expanse," Nuria says.
"The problem here is that our salaries are very low and life is very expensive."
The wider cost of living is the second most important issue for Spaniards, according to numerous surveys carried out during this election period.
Wages failing to catch up with rising prices – despite Spain's GDP growing faster than the three bigger EU countries, Germany, France and Italy – is another reason why Sánchez's PSOE party is only sitting in second place, according to final opinion polls.
Feijóo is said to be most likely to form the next government with the support of Vox under its leader Santiago Abascal.
Having called access to housing a "vital emergency", Feijóo wants to cut taxes for under-40s buying their first home and scrap the Socialists' housing law.
Pedro Sánchez (left) and Núñez Feijóo on screen during the leaders' debate
On housing, Vox has gone further than PSOE and PP, promising to prioritise Spaniards over foreigners for social housing and housing aid, as well as other welfare benefits.
On immigration, identified as the third most important issue, Vox advocates deportations for criminals from abroad and, most controversially, a policy of remigration for foreign nationals who "do not contribute to Spain".
Daniel, 30, is unemployed and says he is ready to vote for Vox for the first time
Opponents of Vox say those who have arrived legally and live and work peacefully risk being forced out.
But 30-year-old Daniel, who is currently unemployed, says he is ready to give his vote to Vox for the first time.
"First of all, it's immigration. It's bad in Spain today – that's why I'm going further to the right," he says.
"The left helps those who don't work, but we need people who work and contribute. We need to give less aid to people who come from abroad and don't contribute."
"We are almost being charged to just breathe at the moment," he says.
We meet Daniel coming out of a shopping centre. We explain that other people we met in the previous hour who told us they support Vox did not want to give their name or be photographed.
Is he proud to be voting far right, or does he have concerns about his choice?
"I'll say it like it is… I've always been centre right but have gone to the extreme right… I've decided to choose nationalism."
Spain's control of its borders was criticised by 22 of its 26 EU partners in the summer, in a rebuke to Sánchez.
In July more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory of Ceuta in just two days.
Sánchez has argued the foreign workforce is essential to Spain's economic growth, and in April announced plans to give half a million undocumented migrants legal status.
Maria and German feel they have little choice but to back the Socialist party
In the final days of the campaign, Sánchez has made a flurry of new spending announcements amounting to billions of euros, promising wage rises in the public sector, higher pensions and discounted transport.
Twenty-year-old student María García says she welcomes the promises but asks why they have come so late in the day.
"The Socialist party have been in power for eight years and now suddenly, during the election campaign, they are passing a lot of progressive laws – which I agree with – but isn't that hypocritical?" she says.
"I don't really have a choice but to vote for them, but come on – you had eight years to do all this!"
Maria's sentiments chime with those of her boyfriend German Martinez, 18.
I put it to them that nearly a fifth of Spaniards are said to be choosing Vox and a number of studies say it's set to be the top choice of first-time voters.
"I believe Spain is stepping into the lion's den because we are scared of the dogs outside. We need to be careful," she says.
"People need to inform themselves – just listen to what these guys say. That 20% of Spanish people agree with them really scares me."
Sánchez will be hoping that fear among the undecided of a national government that includes Vox will save him.
He is a great political survivor, but even if his party wins the most votes he has no obvious path to build a majority.
The man who called a snap election over housing now faces his own eviction - from office.

Matt Handbury, nephew of Rupert Murdoch, admits making offensive remark and says he was referencing assault survivor’s ‘strikingly attractive get-up’
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
A former Murdoch media executive has admitted he said Grace Tame “must be looking to be raped again” at an event, after the former Australian of the year overheard the comment and confronted him.
Tame, a child sexual assault victim survivor who was Australian of the year in 2021 for her advocacy work, revealed in an opinion piece for Crikey that she heard Matt Handbury make the comment to another man at a function last week.
“That’s Grace Tame. Look at her with her tits hanging out. She must be looking to be raped again,” Handbury said, according to Tame’s piece published on Friday.
Tame wrote that she didn’t realise that the man was Handbury until a bystander told her. He introduced himself as “Matt” after she confronted him.
The 77-year-old is Rupert Murdoch’s nephew and the former owner of Murdoch Magazines and Murdoch Books. He is now on the board of The Sydney Retreat, a rehab centre.
Tame said Handbury conceded at the UNSW event – where former military lawyer David McBride was presented with an award – that he had made the comment.
The following day, Handbury sent an email to Tame, seen by Guardian Australia, in which he also admitted he said “she must be looking to be raped again”. Tame was 15 when repeatedly sexually abused by her 58-year-old maths teacher, Nicolaas Bester, who was later convicted and jailed. In 2019, Tame won a supreme court exemption which overturned a Tasmanian law that had until then gagged her from speaking about her experiences of assault.
“He [Handbury] didn’t say she must be looking to get raped,” Tame told Guardian Australia. “He said she must be looking to get raped again . Therefore evidencing his prior knowledge of what I have been through.”
Tame said that the comment “activated really deep seated trauma and there are consequences to that”.
“It’s really destabilising and disorienting because your body is essentially your abused self and it is in total survival mode,” she said.
Handbury said in the email to Tame: “I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up. It was meant to be in appreciation in a male-to-male exchange. I can see that might be offensive in the context of suggesting a woman is making herself attractive to men in some titillating fashion.”
“I also said: ‘She must be looking to be raped again.’ This was certainly meant for no one’s ears but my friend. However it was in poor taste. In fact in highly objectionable taste and I regretted it as soon as I got out into the fresh air. Thank you for calling me out.
“Some men, obviously including myself, are prone to finding suggestive humour in the wrong places. I deeply regret my letting such bad habits get in the way of common courtesy, respect and decency. Please accept my humblest apologies.
“Thank you for opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink on Friday. But no one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous that night.”
Tame wrote in her Crikey piece that “what makes this provocation especially egregious is that Matt didn’t reference an imagined harm, but a very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about”.
“It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?” she wrote.
“This isn’t about Matt personally; it’s about a broader culture of normalised violence. However, part of that culture is the self-censorship that protects people like him.”
Tame referred to research that suggested 35% of Australian men believe women’s rights have come too far, adding that “research has repeatedly shown that misogynistic attitudes are a broad predictor of violent extremism and prevalent among men of all ages.”
Tame told Guardian Australia she often faced re-traumatising behaviour from men.
“I’m tired. I’m tired of the maltreatment. I’m tired of the gaslighting. I’m tired of being baited and then have people be shocked why I would be angry or re-traumatised,” she said on Friday.
Tame thanked bystanders at the event who supported her following Handbury’s comment.
The chief executive of Full Stop Australia, Karen Bevan, called on people to speak up if they heard similar comments because “we all have the power to shift this”.
“If one of the most recognised survivor advocates in the country can be spoken about like this at an event honouring a whistleblower in a room full of people, you can be assured this behaviour is normalised,” Bevan said.
“Things like this do get said in workplaces, pubs, group chats and boardrooms across the country, where no one is recording, and no one writes about it afterwards.”
Crikey reported Handbury told the outlet in further correspondence that he didn’t recall using the phrase “tits hanging out”.
“It doesn’t sound like me. I think I said something along the lines of ‘Did you see Grace Tame? What a hot outfit’ followed by the terrible reference to rape.”
Handbury was contacted for comment as was The Sydney Retreat.

Tame says her "whole body was prickling with distress" over what Handbury said.
An Australian former media executive has admitted he said a child sex abuse survivor and prominent advocate "must be looking to be raped again" because of the way she was dressed at an event.
Grace Tame, 31, was groomed and abused by a teacher and has been honoured as Australian of the Year in 2021 for her advocacy work on child safety.
In an op-ed for independent media outlet Crikey, Tame said she overheard Matt Handbury speaking to a friend, and was left distressed by the remark and the failure of others who heard it to intervene.
Handbury, nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms, has not responded to a BBC request for comment, but in an email to Tame said he regretted the "highly objectionable" comment as soon as he said it.
Matt Handbury is the nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms
Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she had heard him correctly.
She said the encounter at the University of New South Wales event last week triggered flashbacks to her abuse and left her feeling like she would vomit.
"My whole body was prickling in distress," she wrote for Crikey.
"The many men and women who'd seen the confrontation were incredulous, and quick to express their anger at Matt's behaviour... Ironically though, in a room full of seasoned activists, journalists, lawyers and actual whistleblowers, not one person besides me took Matt to task in the heat of the moment."
The next day, in an email seen by the BBC, Handbury, 77, apologised for the "attempt at humour in less than poor taste".
"I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up... I also said: 'She must be looking to be raped again.'
He thanked her for "calling me out" and "opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink".
"But no-one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous last night," he said, before signing off.
Handbury ran Murdoch Magazines for 13 years after buying the business from his uncle in 1991. He sold it to Seven Network's subsidiary Pacific Publications in 2004.
Tame said Handbury's remarks were "especially egregious" because it referenced a "very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about" rather than an "imagined harm".
"It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?"
From the age of 15, Tame was groomed and raped by her 58-year-old maths teacher Nicolaas Ockert Bester. He was later found guilty and served one year and nine months in jail for sexually abusing Tame when she was his student in 2011.
"They're not always as extreme, public or evidenced, but these kinds of experiences are part of my everyday life," Tame wrote on Instagram of Handbury's remarks.
"I'm tired of the maltreatment; and the gaslighting that follows. Tired of being provoked, then asked why I'm angry.
"I'm tired of copping more flak for fighting injustice than those who mete it out."
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line .

Dropping of corruption charges against Israeli PM after unusual intervention could set damaging precedent
The Israeli judges presiding over Benjamin Netanyahu’s corruption trial have called on prosecutors to end proceedings, a highly unusual intervention that leaves the attorney general facing a momentous political decision.
The prime minister has been charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three complex and overlapping criminal cases that hinge on his relationship with telecoms magnates and other wealthy businessmen. Ending the trial without a ruling could set damaging precedents for media independence and how politicians are held to account.
“There were evidentiary difficulties in the case, but the position the judges laid out effectively means abandoning the media to the whims of politicians and publishers, and setting an impossible bar for conviction in corruption cases,” said Yael Freidson, the legal correspondent for Haaretz, who has covered the trial since it began in 2020.
The judges urged prosecutors to drop one case because “the chances of a conviction are low”, seek a plea deal in a second, and reconsider the third set of charges. Even if prosecutors were to prove the allegations of fraud and breach of trust in that case, it was not clear that Netanyahu’s alleged behaviour amounted to criminal conduct, they said.
The attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, who was summoned to court to hear the judges’ statement in person, must now decide whether to accept their recommendations and end a trial that has dominated and shaped Israeli politics for the best part of a decade.
The decision is not straightforward, even though the current bench has in effect indicated a not guilty verdict is a foregone conclusion. If the trial continues, their ruling could still be appealed to a higher court, where fresh judges could take a different stance.
“[The former prime minister] Ehud Olmert was acquitted on all charges by the district court and was subsequently convicted by the supreme court on a minor charge,” Ben Caspit wrote in Maariv. “It ain’t over till it’s over.”
“[Baharav-Miara] could opt to reach a lenient plea bargain agreement with the defendant and put it all to rest, but that would be an admission of the entire justice system’s failure and would further fuel the conspiracy theories that Netanyahu and his disciples have been pumping ever since he was indicted.”
Settling or dropping all charges would immediately and permanently absolve Netanyahu, ending the threat of jail time and dispelling the legal shadow hanging over his political future.
A bill making its way through the opposition-controlled parliament would in effect bar him from serving as prime minister until the trial was concluded.
Netanyahu, who has pleaded not guilty to all charges, claims he is the victim of a political witch-hunt and welcomed the judges’ recommendation as a vindication. “The truth has finally come to light,” he said.
Baharav-Miara has withstood pressure from the judges in the case twice before. In 2023 and in 2025 they urged prosecutors to drop bribery charges, the most serious ones that Netanyahu faces, although they stopped short of suggesting the whole trial should be wrapped up.
Perhaps the single point of agreement between Netanyahu’s supporters and his critics in relation to the trial is concern that it has been allowed to drag on for too long. Testimony from Netanyahu had extended over a year and a half, across 98 hearings, the longest by a single witness in Israeli judicial history, Freidson said. The transcripts from all the hearings run to more than 60,000 pages.
Oren Persico has sat in every hearing since the case began in 2020, covering it for the investigative magazine The Seventh Eye. Over that period he watched the judges slowly lose control of their courtroom, he said.
“It started with giving the defence a lot of rope to do what they wanted. Netanyahu’s lawyer lashed out at the prosecution and humiliated them, almost every day, and attacked the judges, which should be an absolute red line in court,” he said. “I think the judges are afraid and tired; they just want to get it all over with.”
The sense of a bench cracking under pressure was exacerbated by the recommendation to reconsider charges in one of the cases against Netanyahu. These were laid out by prosecutors seven years ago, and have not changed since, prompting joking questions about whether the judges had even read the indictment, and serious ones about their political judgment.
When Netanyahu was indicted, he decided to fight the charges both inside and outside the courtroom, declaring war on the prosecution, the media, the police and key democratic and judicial institutions, Persico said.
“To keep himself out of jail, he tried to form an authoritarian state here in Israel, which tore apart society. I understand the interest in putting an end to that,” Persico said. “But ending the trial would send a terrible message to criminals and politicians and media bosses: that if you fight strongly enough you can get away with anything.”

Watch: Zelensky questions "strange" Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.
In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.
"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.
Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced .
Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.
Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.
So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.
The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.
Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal."
He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin.
"You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."
The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.
"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.
He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.
Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.
"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."
Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.
On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.
Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".
He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.
But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.
Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.
Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.
"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez said on Friday that he was convinced he would ⁠secure a left-wing majority ⁠in a snap ​general election despite adverse public polling, as the political parties prepared to wrap up campaigning ahead of Sunday’s vote, Reuters reported.
Amid a legal ban on publishing new ⁠opinion surveys, the Socialist leader insisted that internal data suggested his party would win the most votes, allowing him to clinch re-election with the support of smaller ⁠leftist allies.
“I can’t conceive of us losing,” Sanchez told radio station SER, adding that left-leaning voters were ​increasingly mobilising to turn out in droves, a ‌prerequisite for reaching a progressive ‌majority to tackle issues such as the country’s deep housing crisis.
double quotation mark “When progressive Spain gets going, it’s unstoppable.”
However, nearly all the polls released before ‌the ban showed a clear advantage for a potential coalition between the conservative People’s Party and far-right Vox, which seek to oust Sanchez after eight years in power.
In other news, budget carrier Norse Atlantic said on Friday it would ⁠file a petition for bankruptcy for ⁠its main Norwegian operating ​unit, becoming the latest airline to succumb to soaring fuel costs wrought by the war ⁠in Iran.
“ Norse Atlantic has stopped flying. All flights operated by Norse Atlantic Airways AS and Norse Atlantic UK Ltd from 27 November at 14.00 CET are cancelled. This includes return flights. Please do not go to the airport for a cancelled flight ,” the company said in a statement on its website.
The airline failed to pay its employees’ November salaries this week, a pilot union said Thursday, as reported by AFP.
Norse is the ⁠second European ​airline to enter bankruptcy proceedings this year after Latvia’s airBaltic, highlighting the toll of the Iran war on carriers that entered the crisis without fuel hedges ⁠as jet fuel prices surged, Reuters noted.
The company said it had not been able to secure sufficient funding to meet its short-term liquidity needs, with the board deciding ⁠to file a bankruptcy petition on 27 November with the Agder District Court in Norway for its ​operating subsidiary.
As mass protests over a nationwide housing crisis have forced Sánchez into an early general election, the Guardian travelled to Spain’s Andalusian coast to find out what’s driving the housing crisis, what solutions are on offer and why rightwing populists are gaining ground.
In Spain, the parties are set to hold their closing rallies this evening, ​with the Socialists ‌and the Broad ​Front choosing Madrid for their ​events.
Meanwhile, the PP and Vox have opted for Seville and Valencia.
Spaniards observe a “day of reflection” on the eve of the vote. Campaigning, rallies and political advertising are banned so voters can weigh their choices before heading to the polls.
Freelance journalist based in Madrid and host of the Sobremesa podcast
Vox has often been portrayed in international coverage as a party of Franco nostalgists whose ultraconservative Catholicism and civil-war rhetoric towards the separatist Catalan “enemy within” threatened a return to the worst of Spain’s recent past.
Yet since its disappointing showing at the 2023 general election, Abascal has purged much of the party’s original leadership and overseen an ideological renewal.
In looking to update its messaging, Vox has blended elements of Marine Le Pen’s welfare chauvinism , such as the concept of “national priority”, with ideas coming from the pan-European, white nationalist identitarian movement.
Virtually absent from Spanish political debate a year ago, national priority would give Spaniards preferential access to social housing, public services and welfare benefits, with Vox already securing PP backing for the principle in regional coalition deals.
In September, however, the European Commission warned that even the residence-based criteria used at a regional level could discriminate against citizens of other EU member states. Vox’s general election manifesto goes further, pledging to exclude all non-Spanish citizens from the country’s minimum-income benefit.
If the polls are right, PP’s Alberto Núñez Feijóo could become prime minister on a lower vote share than the PP secured in the last election. He would then owe his majority to Vox’s surge and support in coalition, and Abascal would have both the leverage and the incentive to show his voters what the party can deliver in office.
A coalition formed on those terms could also foreshadow a closer alliance between conservatives and the far right at a European level. A Le Pen victory in the French presidential election next spring would put the nationalist right at the head of one of the EU’s two most influential states, shifting the political centre of gravity in Brussels and opening the way for a durable governing bloc to the right of the EU’s traditional grand coalition.
It was not by chance that Vox opened its election campaign with a rally displaying video messages of support from Le Pen, Meloni and AfD’s Alice Weidel. Having drawn on its far-right European allies to reinvent itself, Vox could now in turn strengthen their hand if it is successful in becoming the PP’s kingmaker after Sunday’s vote.
Sánchez’s defeat would also deprive the centre left of its strongest counterweight in the European Council, where he is the only social democrat to represent one of the EU’s major powers.
Speaking to the Vox rally, Weidel proclaimed: “All of Europe is waiting for a political change in Madrid.” All of Europe may not be waiting for such a change, but it is certainly watching.
Sitting on a park bench, taking in the sunny day, Naima reflected on all that had seemingly changed since she moved to Spain three decades earlier.
Back then, the Moroccan national had felt warmly welcomed by Spaniards. “I had never, at any point in my life, felt like there was racism,” she said.
“But now things are changing. And the blame lies with rightwing politics.”
Over the years, she has steadily watched as a growing crop of politicians sought to win votes by demonising migrants, minorities and Muslims. The impact reverberated deeply in places such as Torre-Pacheco, whose fertile fields and constant demand for farmhands has long attracted workers from around the world.
“They peddle racism, and lots of people end up suffering,” said Naima, 53. “Here everyone knows me, but others speak of being treated differently, looked at in a certain way, or having gestures made at them.”
On Sunday, Spain is set to gain a glimpse of how deeply engrained these divisions have become as voters cast their ballots in a snap general election.
Most polls suggest the government of the Socialist leader, Pedro Sánchez, will be replaced by a rightwing coalition led by the conservative People’s party (PP) and supported by the far-right, anti-immigration Vox party.
If so, it will be the first time that a far-right party has governed Spain since the return to democracy after the death of General Franco.
No new polls are allowed to be published in Spain in the five days before a Spanish election, but one company has found a surprising solución alternativa.
The Adelaide Review ran from 1984 to 2020, covering the city’s cultural and artistic life until Covid and upheavals in the media world made it “untenable”, its editor, Amanda Pepe , wrote in the final edition .
But now it has found unexpected new life as an, erm, back passage for Spanish polls in the blackout period.
The Review site is now owned by a company called Prensa Ibérica, which also runs the Spanish newspaper El Periódico.
An article on the Periódico website that links to the poll criticises “outdated legislation” that lets political parties see polls, but not citizens.
“The Adelaide Review’s daily poll addresses this issue, giving citizens access to the same information used by politicians,” it said.

New Zealand's final vote count has left neither bloc with a majority, handing a brand-new centrist party the power to decide who governs.
The Electoral Commission's final tally showed more support for minor parties on the ideological flanks than before. A total of 2.8 million votes were cast.
The tally on Friday, after 400,000 special votes including ballots from New Zealanders abroad, showed Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's National party dropping two seats to finish on 40.
The right-wing bloc now holds 65 seats in the 130-seat parliament, one short of the 66 needed. The left, led by Labour's Chris Hipkins, has 58, with Labour on 36.
That leaves the Opportunity party, an unaligned centrist newcomer with seven seats, as kingmaker. Its support would not be enough to put the left in power, Hipkins conceded on Friday, in an apparent admission of defeat.
Luxon, who ruled out working with Opportunity before the 7 November vote, reversed course saying he was confident of forming a government with Opportunity and his usual partners, the libertarian ACT (13 seats) and the populist NZ First (12).
"These negotiations may be challenging and they could take some time," he said. "But getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly."
Opportunity is led by 38-year-old business consultant Qiulae Wong, who has said she could work with either side. Her party's five "bottom line" policies include tougher climate action and an end to bottom-trawling, both at odds with ACT and NZ First.
Wong also repeated that she will not join a government in which NZ First leader Winston Peters is foreign minister, citing his past remarks in parliament about Asian people. She said she would consider either a full coalition or a "confidence and supply" deal, under which her MPs would back key legislation and decide other bills case by case.
Both major parties took under 30% of the party vote: Labour 29.88% and National 28.35%. Analysts pointed to anger over the cost of living and little enthusiasm for either leader.
PM Luxon survived two confidence votes among his own MPs this year, while Hipkins led Labour to defeat in 2023. Minor parties on both flanks gained ground, with the Greens on 17 seats and Te Pati Māori on five.
Opportunity's rise is striking: it failed three times to enter parliament before Wong took over less than a year ago, and none of its new MPs has served before. If no government can be formed, New Zealand could face a fresh election.

Taiwanese officials raise alarm over interference by China in elections that will shape fortunes of ruling party
Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local elections that will shape the fortunes of the ruling Democratic Progressive party (DPP) as it navigates an increasingly precarious set of relationships on the global stage.
Saturday’s vote will choose mayors, council members and other local leaders across 22 districts. Unlike the presidential elections, in which foreign policy is often a key issue, the local elections, held every four years , are largely focused on bread-and-butter issues such as housing affordability and wealth distribution.
Nevertheless, China looms large over the vote, which takes place against the background of intense military pressure from Beijing . China claims Taiwan as part of its territory despite never having ruled the self-governing island. Taiwanese officials have raised the alarm over thousands of incidents of suspected misinformation or election interference, and certain candidates have been subjected to harassment from the Chinese authorities. There have also been reports of hundreds of China-linked AI-generated videos spreading disinformation about Taiwanese politicians disliked by Beijing.
Beijing calls the allegations of election interference “completely fabricated”. Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for China’s Taiwan affairs office, said the allegations “stir up anti-China sentiment to win votes”.
Wei-Ting Yen, a political scientist at Academia Sinica, Taiwan’s national research academy, said: “Even though local elections are not about China, the outcome of local elections will have huge implications for cross-strait relations.”
Most races are a tight competition between a candidate from the ruling DPP and the main opposition party, the Kuomintang (KMT). The KMT promotes closer ties with Beijing, and its chair, Cheng Li-wun, travelled to China this year to meet Xi Jinping, China’s leader. Xi has vowed to unify China with Taiwan, and has not ruled out using military action to achieve that aim.
Yen said if the KMT loses some of its traditional strongholds, Beijing “may need to reconsider what is the most effective strategy for influencing Taiwanese people”.
One of the most contentious votes is the race for Taipei mayor, an office that the DPP has not held for nearly three decades. The DPP has selected as its challenger Puma Shen, a national legislator whom Beijing declared a “diehard separatist” in 2024. It is the first time a candidate under sanctions by Beijing has run to be mayor of Taiwan’s capital city. In the neighbouring New Tapei City race, the DPP’s Su Chiao-hui is also proving to be a ferocious challenger to the incumbent KMT.
Shen said in a recent interview that even if he didn’t win, the capital’s mayoral race was “a slap to China” because it proved that “democracy works here in Taiwan”.
Huang Bo-kai, a 23-year-old law student, said his top concern was cross-strait relations and how US-China relations were evolving. “The world’s three major powers are increasingly willing to flex their muscles: the US attacking Iran, Russia attacking Ukraine. I think Taiwan could very well be the next target [of China],” he told the Guardian.
Taiwan’s president, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te, is detested by Beijing and has taken a bolshier stance on cross-strait relations than his predecessor, Tsai Ing-wen, who was admired for her ability to drum up support in Washington while walking a delicate tightrope to avoid angering China.
Lai has pushed for greater spending on weapons to deter military aggression from China. The government has proposed a record 18% increase in defence spending for next year, including for drones and missiles, taking it above 1tn Taiwan dollars (£23bn) for the first time.
But many Taiwanese voters would rather that money was spent on more immediate economic issues. Lev Nachman, a political scientist at National Taiwan University, said the national leaders of the DPP and KMT had been notably absent from the mayoral races, reflecting the extent to which campaigns were focused on local issues.
Going into the campaigns for the 2028 presidential elections, Lai would “try to take advantage of the momentum that [Shen] and Su have built for the DPP,” Nachman said, noting that support for those candidates would not necessarily translate into support for Lai.
Tony Yeh, a Taipei man in his 70s, said: “To put it simply, the authorities should do more to boost the economy and buy fewer weapons.”
Taiwan’s economy has boomed this year, largely thanks to the pivotal role that its semiconductor industry plays in the global artificial intelligence rally. The economy grew by more than 14% in the first nine months of the year, the fastest rate in 50 years. But nearly 70% of workers earned less than the average monthly wage of 49,152 Taiwan dollars (£1,137) in the same period.
Yeh said: “Most traditional industries are having a really tough time.”
William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “The issues that really are going to determine their votes are livelihood issues including the stagnant wage, the astronomically high housing price, the affordability issue, and how the government can better make sure Taiwan’s incredible economic boom fuelled by the global AI growth is going to be distributed more evenly.”
Other voters have more niche concerns. Walking her dog in a park, Kuo Wei-tong, a nail salon worker, said policies affecting pets were among her top concerns.
“People are having fewer children and getting more cats and dogs,” she said. “I think that’s something worth giving serious consideration to as well.”

Incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon loses majority and needs support of Opportunity party to remain in power, or country faces another election
The final results of New Zealand’s general election show the incumbent rightwing coalition will need the support of a centrist newcomer party to form a government, and to avoid sending the country back to the polls.
Preliminary results on 7 November handed the National party and its two coalition partners, the populist New Zealand First and libertarian Act parties, a slim two-seat majority, making the election too close to call until final votes were tallied.
On Friday, the electoral commission released the results from nearly 485,000 “special votes” – those cast from overseas or outside a voter’s electorate. National dropped two seats to 40, Labour stayed on 36 seats, the Greens picked up one seat to 17, Act had 13, New Zealand First 12, Opportunity seven and Te Pati Māori five.
The National-led bloc currently has 65 seats. In the 130-seat parliament, 66 seats are needed for a majority.
The revised results mean the National-led coalition has the only realistic path to power – if it can negotiate a deal with Opportunity. If it cannot, New Zealand will probably need to hold another election.
Three electorate seats changed hands after the special votes. Labour won Wairarapa off National with just 81 votes, and took Hamilton East from National with 173 votes. The Greens won Wellington Bays from Labour with 1,610 votes.
If National applies for a recount and wins back just one of those seats, it could return to power with a slim majority and without needing Opportunity. Applications for a recount must be made by 3 December, and results could take another five days.
Special votes in previous elections have favoured the left, and typically have cost the right one or two seats. Until Friday, a question mark hung over whether National would be able to govern comfortably alongside its coalition partners, or whether it would be forced to cut a deal with the Opportunity party – a newcomer centrist party that incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon had previously ruled out working with.
After the election, Luxon softened his stance on his initial rule-out, saying he intended to find common ground with the Opportunity party.
On Friday afternoon, Luxon said National will now begin formal negotiations with New Zealand First, Act and Opportunity, but he cautioned discussions would be “challenging” and could take some time.
“Getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly,” Luxon said. “Kiwis won’t thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart, or for sending them back to the polls.”
Lara Greaves, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington, said the prospect of New Zealand heading back to the polls was unprecedented, because negotiations between the four parties will be so complex.
“It’s not a 0% chance, it’s the highest chance we’ve ever had of it being another election,” she said.
Opportunity, led by Auckland businesswoman Qiulae Wong , has long said it will negotiate first with the party that secures the highest number of seats.
After the final results were announced, Wong confirmed she would speak with Luxon and that her party’s bottom-lines – which include climate and environment policies and capping political donations – were non-negotiable.
The party would focus on bringing New Zealanders a stable government, Wong told media, and she did not rule out heading back to the polls.
“Clearly stability is important. But setting that more hopeful and aspirational vision, where we can come together as much as possible as New Zealanders and move forward, I think is the priority,” she said.
Having Opportunity in parliament was a “pivotal moment” for the country, Wong said.
“I have every expectation that we will get in there and we will deliver, regardless of what shape the government takes.”
Previously, Wong has said its vision for a low-emissions future, and an inclusive New Zealand, will drive its final decision . Its five bottom-line issues include action on New Zealand’s supermarket duopoly, capping political donations, a 10-year cross-party plan for health, ending bottom trawling in the fishing industry and strengthening New Zealand’s climate commitments.
Negotiations with Opportunity could hit a snag with National’s coalition partner New Zealand First. On Friday, Wong confirmed she would not strike a deal if New Zealand First’s leader, the veteran politician Winston Peters, serves as foreign affairs minister – a position he has held on three occasions.
“We think that his behaviour over successive governments is not the kind of behavior that we expect of someone in that position,” she said.
In other points of tension, New Zealand First and Act have diametrically opposed climate policies, and Act are also unlikely to back Opportunity’s drive for political donation reforms.
Greaves said the Opportunity party will have to make difficult decisions over what it is prepared to gain, or lose. “For minor parties, it’s really hard to go into coalition, or be seen as being too close to a major party or propping up a government, and then turn around later and sell their brand ... as separate from that [major] party.”
Labour leader Chris Hipkins said he was proud the party had gained the highest share of the party vote, but was disappointed it could not deliver a change of government.
It is the second election Hipkins has lost, raising questions over his political future. Hipkins said a decision over his leadership would be made after a government had been formed.
New Zealand could be facing weeks of negotiations in what could become its first ever four-party coalition. In 2023, negotiations took five weeks. With Christmas just four weeks away, New Zealand may need to wait until 2027 to know the shape of its next government.

Türkiye Musiki Eseri Sahipleri Meslek Birliği (MESAM), 1986 yılında başlayan 40 yıllık hak ve telif mücadelesini gala gecesiyle kutladı. İstanbul Lütfi Kırdar Kongre Merkezi Rumeli Salonu’nda düzenlenen MESAM 40’ıncı Yıl Gala Programı ve Ödül Töreni , müzik sektörünün dünü ile bugününü buluşturdu.
MESAM’ın 40 yıllık köklü yolculuğunu anlatan özel tanıtım filmiyle başlayan gece, KARAF Konseri ile müzik ziyafetine dönüştü. Yemekli gala programında Arabeskten Rap’e, Pop’tan Rock’a, halk müziğinden Türk sanat müziğine kadar müziğin her rengi ve her kuşağı tek bir çatı altında buluştu.
Gecenin açılış konuşmasını yapan MESAM Yönetim Kurulu Başkanı Recep Ergül, kurumun 40 yıllık fikri mülkiyet mücadelesinin uluslararası arenadaki büyük başarısına dikkat çekti. Ergül, konuşmasında şu ifadelere yer verdi:
"Türkiye’nin ilk ve en büyük müzik meslek birliği olan MESAM bugün 40 yaşında. Kırk yıldır bu topraklarda fikri mülkiyet ve eser sahipleri adına kararlı bir mücadele yürütüyoruz. MESAM’ın ortaya koyduğu vizyoner çalışmalar, ülkemizin Uluslararası Yazar ve Besteciler Konfederasyonu (CISAC) verilerinde son sıralardan kurtularak 32’nci sıraya kadar yükselmesini sağladı. 40’ıncı yılımız anısına gerçekleştirdiğimiz bu görkemli tören, sanatın birleştirici gücünün toplumumuza en güçlü yansımasıdır. Bugün burada, farklı kuşakların ve farklı müzik türlerinin kucaklaştığı eşsiz bir Türkiye mozaiğinin buluşmasına tanıklık ediyoruz."
ZEKİ MÜREN’DEN SEMİCENK’E, FAZIL SAY’DAN SAGOPA KAJMER’E: TEK ÖLÇÜT EMEK VE LİYAKAT
MESAM 40’ıncı Yıl Ödülleri’nde değerlendirmeler yalnızca başarı, sanatsal üretim, eserlerin kalıcılığı ve sektöre verilen emek temelinde yapıldı. Gecede; büyük yapım şirketleriyle çalışan sanatçılar da bağımsız müzisyenler de aynı hakkaniyet anlayışıyla onurlandırıldı.
Gecede üç ana kategoride toplam 35 ödül takdim edildi. Güncel üretimi ve yüksek etkiyi simgeleyen 18 Başarı Ödülü, Türk müziğine adanmış ömür boyu katkıyı onurlandıran 13 Onur Ödülü ve MESAM’ın kurumsal çalışmalarına destek veren kurum ve isimlere sunulan 4 Teşekkür Ödülü sahiplerini buldu.
MESAMdan 40ıncı yıla özel gece Fazıl Saydan Sagopa Kajmere 35 ödül sahiplerini buldu
Zeki Müren , Mahzuni Şerif, Yıldırım Gürses, Yusuf Hayaloğlu ve Atilla Özdemiroğlu gibi müzik tarihimize silinmez izler bırakan ustalar saygıyla anılırken; ödülleri aileleri ve yasal temsilcileri tarafından alkışlar eşliğinde teslim alındı. Gecede Fazıl Say ve Hakkı Bulut gibi dev isimlerin yanı sıra Semicenk, Mabel Matiz, Gazapizm, Burak Bulut ve Sagopa Kajmer gibi günümüzün öne çıkan sanatçıları da ödüllerine kavuştu.

Bakanlıktan yapılan açıklamaya göre, Bina Yangın Yönetmeliği ile binaların tasarım, yapım, denetim ve kullanım aşamalarında alınması gereken tedbirler güncel ihtiyaçlara göre yeniden düzenlendi.
Yeni düzenlenen yönetmelikte, kapalı otoparklarda elektrikli araç şarj sistemlerine ilişkin doğrudan dış ortama giriş ve çıkışı bulunan katlarda araç kapasitesinin yüzde 20'sine, diğer katlarda ise yüzde 10'una kadar şarj sistemi kurulması esas alındı.
Araçların şarja erişiminin veya fiziki koşulların yeterli olmadığı durumlarda, mahalli itfaiye teşkilatının uygun görüşüyle ilave şarj sistemi kurulabileceği düzenlendi.
Yönetmelikte araçlar için ayrılan şarj alanlarında yangının diğer bölümlere yayılmasını önleyici tedbirler alınması, gerekli durumlarda yangın algılama ve erken uyarı sistemlerinin kurulması da yer aldı.
Acil durumlarda şarj sistemlerinin elektriğini anında kesebilecek acil durum butonu bulundurulması zorunlu hale getirildi.
Yapılarda güneş enerjisine dayalı elektrik üretim sistemlerinin çatı, cephe ve açık otopark üstü uygulamalarında alınması gereken yangın güvenliği tedbirleri yönetmelikte ayrıntılı şekilde belirlendi.
Buna göre, yangın durumunda kaçış güvenliğinin sağlanması, güneş panellerinin yerleşiminde uygun mesafelerin bırakılması, acil durumlar için devre kesici bulundurulması, sistem parçalarına ilişkin uyarı levhalarının yer alması ve bina içinde bulunan sistemlere uygun yangın algılama ve erken uyarı sistemlerinin kurulması zorunlu hale getirildi.
Yapı ruhsatı ve yapı kullanma izin belgesi süreçlerinde yangın güvenliğine yönelik de düzenleme yapıldı.
Buna göre, yangın algılama, söndürme ve tahliye projeleri ile diğer güvenlik önlemleri öncelikle yerel itfaiye teşkilatı tarafından değerlendirilecek.
İtfaiyenin gerekli gördüğü durumlarda yangın güvenlik uzmanlarının da görüşü alınacak. İlgili idareler ancak bu uygunluk görüşünün ardından projeleri inceleyerek onaylayabilecek.
Yeni yönetmelikle yapıların tasarım, inşaat, denetim ve kullanım aşamalarında görev alan kişi ve kurumların yangın güvenliğine ilişkin sorumlulukları da belirlendi.
Bu kapsamda proje hazırlayan mimar ve mühendislerin, imar planı ve yapı projelerini yangın güvenliği kurallarına ve ilgili standartlara uygun hazırlaması zorunlu hale getirildi.
Müteahhitlerin ve şantiye şeflerinin ise inşaat faaliyetlerini yönetmeliğe ve onaylı projeye uygun yürütme yükümlülükleri netleşti.
Proje ve yapım aşamalarında tespit edilen eksiklik ve aykırılıkların bildirilmesi ile gerekli denetimlerin yapılmasına dair sorumluluklar da düzenlendi.
Bina sahipleri, yöneticiler ve işletmecilerin ise yangın güvenlik sistemlerini çalışır durumda tutması, düzenli kontrollerini yaptırması ve gerekli güvenlik önlemlerini alması zorunlu tutuldu.
Ayrıca yangın güvenlik sistemlerinin bakım ve muayenesini yapan kişiler ile ilgili idarelerin ve yerel itfaiye teşkilatının görev sınırları tanımlandı.
Yönetmelik kurallarının uygulanamadığı özel nitelikli yapılarda ise uluslararası standartların kullanılabilmesine imkan tanındı.
Engelli, yaşlı ve hareket kısıtlılığı bulunan vatandaşların yangın anında binadan güvenle tahliye edilebilmesi için yeni düzenlemeler yapıldı.
Yeni düzenlemeyle yangın güvenlik holü, kaçış merdiveni ve korunumlu koridor gibi kaçış alanlarında özel tahliye bekleme noktaları oluşturulacak.
Bu alanlarda görme engelliler için Braille yazılı yönlendirme işaretleri bulunacak ve yardım çağrısı yapılabilmesi için acil durum butonu ya da sesli iletişim cihazı yerleştirilecek.
Ayrıca yönetmelikle yapı yüksekliği 30,5 metreyi aşan mevcut konutlarda otomatik yangın algılama ve uyarı sistemlerinin kurulması zorunlu hale getirildi.

Beşiktaş , UEFA Avrupa Ligi'nde Gürcistan'ın Batum kentinde İsrail ekibi Hapoel Beer-Sheva'yı 2-1 mağlup etti. Tribünlerde yaşanan olaylar ve maç sonundaki Filistin'e destek görüntüleri geceye damgasını vurdu. TFF Başkanı İbrahim Hacıosmanoğlu da CNN Türk canlı yayınına bağlanarak İsrail takımları, UEFA ile temasları ve olası cezalar hakkında konuştu.
Siyah beyazlıların olayların gölgesinde geçen gecede aldığı sonuç, TFF cephesinde de karşılık buldu. CNN Türk yayınında Beşiktaş camiasına destek veren Hacıosmanoğlu, tribündeki taraftarlar ve sahadaki oyuncular için şu ifadeleri kullandı:
'Beşiktaş taraftarına geçmiş olsun. Galibiyet için Beşiktaş futbolcularının gözlerinden öpüyorum. İyi bir ders verdiler.'
Batum'da yaşananların ardından UEFA ve güvenlik yetkilileriyle konuşan TFF Başkanı, girişimlerin sürdüğünü belirtti. Avrupa futbolundaki dengelere ve İsrail federasyonuna da değinen Hacıosmanoğlu şu açıklamayı yaptı:
'UEFA ve polis yetkilileriyle görüştüm. 55 tane federasyon var, sadece İsrail'in federasyon başkanı ile görüşmedim. Onların bir lobisi yok orada. Yönetimde birinin olması önemli değil, biz istediğimizi yaptırıyoruz. Girişimlerimiz devam ediyor. Beşiktaş taraftarını tebrik ederim.'
İsrail takımlarının Türkiye'de maç yapmasına karşı olduğunu açıkça dile getiren Hacıosmanoğlu, İsrail'in futboldan men edilmesi gerektiğini UEFA toplantılarında savunduğunu anlatırken şu sözleri kullandı:
'İsrail bebek katili, UEFA toplantılarında söyledim. Bunların futboldan atılması gerektiğini de çok kez dile getirdim. Bir önce Beşiktaş maçına, İsrail takımı ile oynadıkları, kafile ile gitmiştim. Bir devlet politikamız var, İsrail takımlarını Türkiye'ye biz istemiyoruz.'
TFF Başkanı, Beşiktaş'ın karşılaşmayı İstanbul 'da oynamak istemesi ihtimali için de şu değerlendirmeyi yaptı:
'Beşiktaş, İstanbul'da oynamak isteseydi, UEFA buna izin verirdi. İsrail takımı gelmezse, hükmen mağlup olurdu. UEFA güvenlik gerekçesiyle maçı başka bir ülkede oynatmak gibi gaflete düşmez. Zaten başkan dostumuz, Türkiye'ye karşı böyle bir şey içerisinde olamazlar.'
Hacıosmanoğlu, Türkiye'nin güvenliği sağlayabileceğini vurgulayıp sözlerini şöyle sürdürdü:
'Bebek katili bir ülkenin takımı bu topraklarda oynayamaz! UEFA sadece güvenlik ister. Bizim devletimiz güvenliği sağlar, İstanbul'da maç oynanırdı ama biz bu ülke topraklarına gelmelerini istemiyoruz.'
Bitiş düdüğünden sonra Beşiktaşlı futbolcular Filistin'e destek pankartının önünde fotoğraf çektirdi, Ouattara da Filistin bayrağını UEFA yazısının üzerine astı. Bu görüntüler olası bir yaptırım ihtimalini akıllara getirdi. Tribünlerdeki olaylar ile bayrak konusunu birbirinden ayıran Hacıosmanoğlu, ceza sorusuna şu yanıtı verdi:
'Taşkınlıklardan ufak cezalar olabilir. Ancak Filistin bayrağı nedeniyle ceza gelmesi söz konusu değil.'
